definition: The collection, inspection and testing, cleaning and redistribution of a product back into the market under controlled conditions (e.g. a formal business undertaking).
Refers to a scenario-based demonstration of the environmental impacts that are avoided by an economy due to the use of value-retention processes (VRPs) within the production mix.
Refers to a constituent part of a broader defined system; an element of a larger whole object that could be a part and/or a product.
Refers to the refurbishment of used equipment that takes place within industrial or factory settings, with a high standard and level of refurbishment.
A previously sold, worn or non-functional product or module, intended for the remanufacturing process.
Refers to the economic impact metrics addressed within this study, specifically: cost advantage ($ USD); and employment opportunity (Full-time equivalent worker, or FTE).
Refers to the carbon dioxide and greenhouse gas equivalent emissions emitted during the extraction and primary processing stages of materials.
Refers to the energy consumed during the extraction and primary processes stages of materials later used as inputs to OEM New and value-retention process production activities.
Refers to the point in the product or object's service life at which the product or object is no longer able to function or perform as required.
Refers to the point in the product or object's service life at which the product may not be needed by the current owner/user, or able to function or perform as required.
Refers to conditions under which certain specified waste shall cease to be waste (per Directive 2008/98/EC).
Refers to the environmental impact metrics addressed within this study, specifically: new material offset (avoided) (kg); embodied material energy (MJ); embodied material emissions.
Refers to the way in which minority group neighbourhoods are burdened with a disproportionate number of hazards, including toxic waste facilities and garbage dumps.
Refers to the manufacturer's expectations about the time period for which a product can be used, usually specified as a median.
Refers to how often something fails, such as a component or system. It is usually expressed in failures per unit of time.
Refers to the traditional flow of products from the point of production through to the consumer and reflects a traditional supply chain management perspective.
Refers to value-retention processes (VRPs) that enable the fulfilment of a completely new life for every usage cycle of the product.
Refers to products in 'active use', including those being repaired for return to the original user.
Refers to products or their components/materials that flow from the circular economic system to the biosphere, and that cannot be recovered.
A technique for the assessment of environmental aspects and potential impacts associated with a product by compiling an inventory of relevant inputs and outputs.
Refers to the choices of a resource circulation in terms of a products life cycle. Major strategies include reuse, refurbish, remanufactured and recycle.
Refers to the consumption usage phase of the product. The lifetime starts at the time of purchase and ends when disposed or replaced.
Refers to a self-contained unit or item, such as an assembly or segment of a larger product, which itself performs a defined task.
Refers to the total 'new' (not reused via value-retention processes (VRPs)) material that is required as inputs to complete each OEM New and Value-Retention Process.
Refers to the manufacturer of the original parts or equipment, including the items manufactured, assembled and installed during construction of a new product.
Refers to traditional linear manufacturing production process activities that rely on 100 per cent new material inputs.
Refers to a piece or segment of an object; may also be a component of a product.
Refers to value-retention processes (VRPs) that enable the completion of, and/or slight extension of, the expected product life.
Refers to the extent to which a product complies with End-of-Waste conditions, and thus qualifies as an input to value-retention processes.
Refers to a hypothetical product life calculation estimated by the manufacturer for which it will honour warranty claims.
Refers to obsolete products awaiting recovery.
Also referred to as virgin material, refers to a material that has not been previously used or consumed, or subjected to processing other than for its original production.
Refers to the carbon dioxide and greenhouse gas equivalent emissions emitted during the OEM New and/or value-retention process production activities.
Refers to direct at-the-meter energy consumed during the OEM New and/or value-retention process production activities.
Refers to an article, object or substance that is manufactured or refined for sale, that is the final output of a process.
Refers to the ability of a product to meet or exceed its original state over time and eliminating the perceived reasons for obsolescence.
Refers to the period that starts at the moment a product completes original manufacture and ends when beyond any reuse or recovery.
Refers to a set of common elements, including underlying technical components, parts or technology that are shared across a range of the company's products.
Refers to the equivalent production shares of OEM New and Value-Retention Processes that are adopted within a sample economy.
Refers to the limit beyond which products or their components cannot be recovered.
Refers to the relevant operations specified in Annex IV B to the Basel Convention. Recycling operations usually involves the reprocessing of waste into products.
Refers to the modification of an object that is a waste or a product to increase or restore performance and/or functionality.
Refers to a standardized industrial process that takes place within industrial or factory settings, in which cores are restored to original as-new condition.
Refers to the fixing of a specified fault in an object that is a waste or a product and/or replacing defective components.
Refers to the using again of a product, object or substance that is not waste, for the same purpose for which it was conceived.
Refers to activities engaged to recapture the value of products, parts, and materials once they have reached end-of-use or end-of-life.
Also referred to as the aftermarket, is a market for used goods or assets, or alternative use for an existing product or asset.
Also referred to as recycled material, refers to any material that has been used at least once before, is not the primary product of a manufacturing or commercial process.
Refers to a product's total lifetime during which it can be used economically or the time during which it is used by one owner.
Refers to non-toxic, highly stable materials that have no negative effects on the natural environment, that are designed to be recovered and reused within production activities.
Refers to the act of raising a product to a higher standard with the objective to improve performance, efficiency, and/or functionality by adding or replacing components.
Refers to the utility gained from a stock of products or service for the period of duration of their lifetime.
Refers to the value of the product based on external factors, such as technology infrastructure changes and attractiveness compared with competing products.
Activities, typically production-type activities, that enable the completion of, and/or potentially extend a product's service life beyond traditional expected service life.
Refers to any substance or object which the holder discards or intends or is required to discard (Directive 2008/98/EC).
Refers to products that go directly from production to disposal and never reach any consumer. Examples include fashion deadstock and imperfect agriculture products.
